questions.q: What do PAGELATCH_UP and PAGELATCH_EX waits on tempdb specifically indicate?
options: Contention among sessions trying to access an allocation page already resident in memory, not a physical disk read
A physical read of a data page from disk into the buffer pool
A row-level lock held by another transaction
A slow client failing to consume returned rows
questions.explain: PAGELATCH waits are latches on in-memory pages — contention to access a page already in the buffer pool, distinct from PAGEIOLATCH's physical disk read wait.

questions.q: What do GAM and SGAM pages track in TempDB?
options: Which extents are allocated at all (GAM) and which mixed extents have at least one free page (SGAM)
The current query plan cache contents
The list of currently blocked sessions
The transaction log's virtual log file boundaries
questions.explain: GAM tracks overall extent allocation; SGAM tracks mixed extents with free space — both are bookkeeping pages every temp-object creation/drop must touch.

questions.q: What is the standard, well-established fix for PAGELATCH contention on TempDB allocation pages?
options: Add multiple TempDB data files, spreading allocation activity across separate files and their own allocation pages
Shrink the TempDB data file as small as possible
Move TempDB onto a single, larger data file
Disable autogrowth on all user databases
questions.explain: Multiple data files distribute the GAM/SGAM/PFS allocation load across separate page sets, directly reducing contention on any single page.

questions.q: Why must all TempDB data files be the same SIZE and FILEGROWTH?
options: SQL Server's proportional-fill algorithm allocates new extents in proportion to each file's free space, so unequal sizes concentrate allocation activity back onto whichever file has more room
SQL Server refuses to start if TempDB files are unequal sizes
Equal sizing is only a cosmetic preference with no functional effect
Unequal file sizes cause TempDB to run out of disk space immediately
questions.explain: Proportional fill favors files with more free space; unequal sizing undoes the benefit of adding multiple files by re-concentrating allocations.

questions.q: A DBA adds four new TempDB files but sizes each at 1 GB while the original 20 GB file keeps autogrowth on. Contention barely improves. What's the most likely reason?
options: The files are unequally sized, so proportional fill keeps favoring the original larger file, defeating the point of spreading allocation load
TempDB simply cannot support more than one data file
PAGELATCH waits are unrelated to file count in any scenario
The fix failed because autogrowth was left enabled on any file at all
questions.explain: With mismatched sizes, proportional fill continues to route most new allocations to the file with more free space, so the contention-reducing effect of adding files doesn't materialize.
